newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Farm ministers oppose planned cereal cuts.
newsitem.headline: Farm ministers oppose planned cereal cuts.

text.p: European Union farm ministers on Monday attacked proposed cuts in cereals subsidies while France called for grain planting curbs to be lifted next year, EU officials said.
The EU's executive Commission has called for a 1.4 billion ecu ($1.6 billion) reduction of cereals payments to help fund aid for beef producers hit by the mad cow crisis.
"Such a decision would unbalance the 1992 reform of the Common Agricultural Policy," French Farm Minister Philippe Vasseur said in a speech.

German Farm Minister Jochen Borchert said cereals cuts were unacceptable because permanent payments had been agreed to compensate farmers for the 1992 price and production cutting reforms and any change would shatter farmers' confidence.

Member states argue that cereals cuts are unnecessary because of savings due to a firmer dollar which has lowered the cost of export subsidies. Payments to farmers for taking land out of production were also less than anticipated.
Finnish Farm Minister Kalevi Hemila said cereals farmers should not have to bear the whole burden of the cuts.
"It's not fair to take only from cereals," he said.
But EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler was adamant, saying the cuts were still needed and that cereals farmers were over-compensated.

France, supported by Britain and several other member states, said the amount of land farmers must set aside in 1998 to qualify for EU subsidies should be reduced to zero, from five percent, to keep exports flowing.
"I consider that only a zero set-aside rate can meet Europe's objectives," Vasseur said.
Vasseur said it was of the utmost priority for France that the set-aside rate is agreed as part of the 1997/98 farm price package and at the latest by June 30, 1997.
The cereals market situation was causing concern, he said, noting stocks were very low.
"Frost in the United States and drought in Europe will not improve matters," he added.
Fischler responded that climatic trends must be studied further before any proposal could be made.
Outside the ministerial meeting some 7,000 Italian farmers staged a colourful protest against EU farm policy.

Waving yellow flags, flying multi-coloured balloons and to the sound of Puccini's opera Tosca, they demanded higher milk production quotas and a bigger share of EU subsidies for wine, olive oil and other Mediterranean farm products.
"Farm prices are falling and farmers' revenues are declining. We want a fairer deal," declared Paolo Micolini, head of the Coldiretti farmers' union, one of Italy's largest.
